What changed in the new Death Star, and why

The current portal has the right capabilities. The redesign changes how they are arranged, so that Thomas can open the platform, see who to call, understand why now, and log the call, all in a few clicks.

Prepared October 2, 2026Compared: the current portal (commit 8f21196, Sept 28) and the clickable prototypeAll data on both sides is fictional
OverviewHomeBrainDashboardDatabaseContactPropertyCalendarVisual styleWhat stays
The short version

The portal stopped being a catalogue of tools and became a daily call surface

When we reviewed the current portal, the first thing a user saw on Home was every tool in it. The most valuable output, the plain-English "why now", was easiest to reach by typing a name into the chat. The redesign puts that output at the center and arranges everything else around it.

31
differently worded "why now" texts on an owner page become one
21

Summary first, detail on request

Every page opens with a sentence or a number. Tables and long records sit inside a tab or one click away, and a section shows about six items before "View all".

Trust before persuasion

A why now never looks more certain than its evidence. Each claim carries one of four statuses, always shown as color, word and icon: Verified, Single source, Stale or Disputed.

One of everything

One why now, one score, one assistant, one place for each destination. Thomas's labels and order stay. The structure changes, the vocabulary does not.

Home

Home now answers one question: who do I call first?

The old Home was a menu. The new Home is a briefing that ends in a single next action.

What changed

  • A greeting with a fact. "22 Class A owners haven't had a call yet" replaces the tile wall.
  • Today's Attack Plan on Home. Three steps, a progress bar (6 of 40 calls) and the buttons Open Attack Plan, Log a call and Build a list.
  • Four numbers instead of twenty-two tiles. Calls today, conversations, Class A coverage and follow-ups due, each with its goal.
  • Brain is open and already working. It says Marchetti is first on today's list and offers Open record.
  • A navy frame. The sidebar and top bar are navy, the work happens on white panels, and the photograph is gone.

Why

  • In discovery, the first message of Home was "here are all the tools". Nothing said who to call or what changed overnight.
  • At least five places competed to start the day: Home, Dashboard, Today, Field Mode and Prospects.
  • Thomas asked for classic corporate, midnight blue, quiet and not data-dense. A photograph behind translucent tiles worked against that.

Better for Thomas

  • He reaches the first owner to call in two clicks, without scrolling.
  • He starts the day from a suggestion, not from a blank page.
  • The builder tools no longer sit next to his daily work, so Home reads as his, not as an admin menu.
Brain

One assistant, available everywhere, with answers you can check

Thomas already treats Brain as the fastest way to get a why now. The redesign makes that official and makes the answer safer to say out loud.

What changed

  • One input. The old page had two message boxes. The new one has a single composer with Ask and Act modes, attachments, @ mentions and slash commands.
  • Brain follows you. Open and docked on Home, a small "Ask Brain" pill on other pages (⌘J), a full page on Brain. It tells you what it is scoped to, for example "Scoped to Home".
  • Structured answers. Filters appear as chips, matching owners as a short list with class badges, followed by sources.
  • Actions ask first. A list is only saved after "Save list" is pressed.
  • Tidier history. Chats are grouped as Pinned, Today, Previous 7 days and Older, with search.

Why

  • Thomas types an owner's name into Brain because the owner record was too slow and gave conflicting answers. The product should meet him there.
  • The portal had several assistants with different names. A single name, Brain, removes the question of which one to ask.
  • His main fear is saying something wrong to an owner. A reminder under the composer says "Brain can be wrong. Check trust badges before you say it out loud."

Better for Thomas

  • No page change to ask a question about what he is looking at.
  • Every answer shows where it came from, so he can decide how much to rely on it.
  • Brain proposes and Thomas approves, so nothing changes in the database by accident.
Prototype note. Brain answers in the prototype are scripted, and Learning Mode is drawn but disabled.
Dashboard · Attack Plan

The day starts from a ranked list, not an empty form

The seven Dashboard tabs keep Thomas's names and order. What changed is what the first tab shows and how the tabs look.

What changed

  • Today's plan lists the owners to call. Each row has the owner, the property, one why-now line, a trust badge and a call button. A line below says "5 Class A owners have no verified reason yet".
  • Goals and meetings sit beside the plan. Daily, weekly and monthly goals, and today's meetings with times.
  • The task form moved down into the to-do list, where it is a small action instead of the whole page.
  • Time travel. A Day and Week stepper with a calendar popover shows a past day as a recap and a future day as a queue.
  • Tabs inside the white panel. Each tab starts with one Brain line, such as "22 Class A owners have no logged call yet and 3 loans mature inside 12 months."
  • Shorter tab names. Conversation Tracker, Listing Activity and Website Analytics become Conversations, Listings and Web analytics. Outreach performance, Reporting and Listings are redrawn as display-only pages.

Why

  • In the recording, Attack Plan opened on an empty task form even though the system knows who should be called.
  • Logging calls was a separate step, and the manual counters were not being kept up to date. The plan and the calls now live in the same place.
  • Metric grids full of zeros hid the few numbers that matter. Goals now show progress against a target.

Better for Thomas

  • He sees who to call, why, and how safe it is to say, before he picks up the phone.
  • The call button is in the row, so the plan and the action are one step apart.
  • The tabs still read the way he knows them, so nothing has to be relearned.
Database

The Database opens on answers, not on a blank area

Contacts and Properties remain the two views. The table now carries the information Thomas used to open each record to find.

What changed

  • A ranked table from the first second. Name, lead property, why now, last touch, trust and score, sorted by score.
  • Filters in one row. Class, trust, signals and "In territory", plus a search for name, phone, email or address.
  • Lists with Recently viewed. The last records opened are one click away, and the lists keep their counts.
  • Peek instead of leave. Selecting a row opens a preview panel. ↑ and ↓ step through the list, Esc closes, and "Open full page" is available when needed.
  • Find anything with ⌘K. Search by name, phone or BBL from any page.
  • Designed edge states. Loading, empty and error screens exist for the table.

Why

  • The old table loaded only after a list was picked, so the first view showed nothing. Thomas had to know what to ask before he could see anything.
  • Records opened as browser-like tabs that piled up under the main tabs. A preview keeps his place in the list.
  • Showing the why now and trust in the row lets him compare owners without opening each one.

Better for Thomas

  • He can scan eleven owners and pick one in seconds.
  • He can check a record and return to the list without losing his place.
  • Search works on the details he actually has during a call: a name, a number or a BBL.
Prototype note. The Prospects view and a few lists (such as Professional grade and Portfolio sellers) are drawn but disabled.
Contact record

One case file, built around a why now Thomas can trust

This is the screen Thomas is on when a call connects. It had to become shorter, faster and consistent.

What changed

  • One why now, one score. The same sentence and the same score (132) appear on Home, Attack Plan, the preview, the case file and Brain.
  • The why now comes first. A Verified badge, the sentence in larger type, driver tags and a "Next: Call" button with the number.
  • "Why this?" shows the proof. Three drivers with their weight, then evidence rows with source, tier, date and a trust badge. Each row has "Flag as wrong".
  • Disputed facts are named. "Mailing address is disputed. It isn't part of this why now." Flagging a fact turns the why now Disputed with "Check before you say it."
  • Tabs replace one long scroll. Overview, Intelligence, Ownership, Activity, Details and History.
  • Notes, Lists and Record in a side rail that stays in view.

Why

  • In the current record we found three differently worded why-now texts and two different scores on the same page. Thomas could not tell which to believe, so he left for Brain.
  • Confidence and freshness mostly lived on admin pages. A stale 2016 loan date looked as current as a 2026 violation.
  • "Missing data is acceptable; incorrect data is not." The screen now follows that rule.

Better for Thomas

  • One glance tells him whether the reason is safe to say out loud.
  • He can open the evidence in one click without leaving the call.
  • He can flag a bad fact immediately, which protects the next call too.

The call happens on the same screen

  • Call starts a timer in a navy band at the top of the page. The why now stays visible below it.
  • End call opens the outcome tray. A no-answer is logged in two clicks.
  • Connected puts the cursor in the notes and adds a card to Conversations.
  • Save shows "Call logged", and "Next owner" moves to the next row of the plan. The calls counter on Home counts up.

In the current portal, the call, the context and the logging happen on different surfaces.

Property record

The building tells the same story as its owner

The current property page already showed evidence with trust labels. The redesign keeps that idea and applies it everywhere, so the building and the owner never disagree.

What changed

  • The owner's why now sits at the top, with "3 lines safe to state" so Thomas knows how much he can say.
  • Evidence has its own tab. Overview, Evidence and Violations are live. Ownership history, Deals, Documents and Permits are drawn as the next tabs.
  • Four compact groups (Building, Use, Debt and capital, Sale and taxes) replace the large grids. Missing values read "Not on record".
  • Owner and portfolio on the right. A Call button for the owner, and the owner's other buildings one click away.
  • Maps move out of the page. The two embedded maps are replaced by a facade photo slot. Maps belong to the Map destination.

Why

  • The old page repeated the same facts in the header, the grids, the why now, the distress signals and the assistant block.
  • Property and owner each had their own score and explanation. Now both read from the same one.
  • A broker thinks in portfolios. Seeing the owner's other buildings supports the call.

Better for Thomas

  • The page fits in one view and does not need a long scroll to find the debt maturity.
  • He can jump from building to owner and back with no change in the story.
  • He can tell a verified fact from a single-source one at a glance.
Dashboard · Calendar

A calendar for planning call blocks, not a copy of Google Calendar

The calendar stays inside Dashboard because it supports the same job as Attack Plan: planning the week.

Two ways to add an event

  • Click an empty slot. A draft event drops in with a small inline card. Enter saves, Esc discards, and "More options" opens the full dialog.
  • New event. A full dialog with duration chips, a calendar choice, a person and notes. A day preview on the right shows what else is scheduled.
  • Overlap warning. "Overlaps Lunch · Grace Okafor (12 PM)" appears before saving, not after.

What changed

  • Colors carry meaning. Meetings are navy, call blocks blue, tours green and marketing amber. Each has a checkbox and a count in the sidebar.
  • The week reads quickly. Today is highlighted, weekends are shaded and a red line marks the current time.
  • A Brain line at the top connects the calendar to the work: "Your 1:30 PM call block has 6 owners queued. Marchetti is first."
  • One primary button. "New event" replaces the Create menu with Event, Task and Out of office.
  • Lighter sidebar. Booking pages and the "Meet with" people search are not part of this proposal.

Why

  • Thomas plans around call blocks, tours and lender calls. The calendar should show that structure, not general-purpose event types.
  • The current version mirrors Google Calendar feature by feature, which adds weight to a tab he opens to plan, not to configure.
  • Double-booking is the common mistake in a busy week, so the warning appears while he is choosing the time.

Better for Thomas

  • Adding a call block takes one click and one key press.
  • The calendar and the plan for the day tell the same story.
  • It matches the look of the rest of the platform instead of a separate dark page.
Prototype note. Existing events are read-only in the prototype. Editing events and connecting a real calendar are not part of this proposal.
Visual style

From a dark, vendor-styled portal to a calm navy frame with white work panels

The new look is not a matter of taste. Each choice answers something Thomas said, or a risk in his daily work: he wants classic corporate and midnight blue, he is not technical, and he is afraid of saying something wrong to an owner.

What changed

  • Navy holds the frame. The sidebar and top bar are navy. All content sits on white panels with a thin border and rounded corners. Navy never appears as a panel inside the content.
  • One typeface, one default size. Inter at 13 pixels for everything in the interface, 16 for the why now, 20 for page titles. The old portal mixed a serif for some greetings and titles with a sans for the rest.
  • Quiet color. Blue is for links and charts. Green, amber, red and grey are used only for status, and always with a word and an icon.
  • One main button per panel. Everything else is an outline or a plain text button.
  • Sentence case. Labels such as "TODAY'S PLAN" and "TASK NAME" in spaced capitals become "Today's plan" and "Task name".
  • Drawn icons, no emoji. One consistent icon set replaces mixed symbols such as the person and building emoji used on record tabs.
  • No photographs, no gradients, except a thin gradient outline on the Ask Brain button, the only one in the product.
  • Light and dark themes. Light is the default. A switch in the account menu changes it, and the navy frame stays the same in both.

Why

  • Thomas asked for classic corporate, midnight blue, sleek and not data-dense. The old portal added orange accents, photography and dark pages beside white ones.
  • In the old portal, tabs flipped between light and dark pages, and every page copied a different vendor: Gmail, Constant Contact, Salesforce, Google Calendar, a chat app. Moving between tabs felt like moving between products.
  • Small grey helper text and spaced capitals are hard to read quickly. A user on the phone all day needs large, plain text where it matters.
  • The style was set by studying three references: Attio for precision and thin borders, Asana for the navy frame and labelled sidebar, and ElevenLabs for the order of Home (greeting, numbers, one detail area).

Better for Thomas

  • The platform looks and behaves like one product, so there is less to relearn on each tab.
  • The eye goes to the one thing that matters: the why now and its status, then the single main action.
  • A familiar, corporate look supports the platform when it is shown to John Stewart and the wider team.
  • Status never depends on color alone, so it reads correctly for color-blind users and in poor light.

Navy and white carry the product. Orange is gone.

Rules that keep it calm

Applied to every new screen.

  • Borders, not shadows, inside panels. Shadows only on things that float, such as menus and dialogs.
  • Zero reads as faded, and unknown values read "Not on record".
  • Disabled changes color only. It stays focusable and says "Not in this proposal yet".
  • Motion explains, never decorates. Panels open and close in about 200 milliseconds, and reduced-motion settings are respected.
  • Accessible by default. AA contrast in both themes, visible focus rings, full keyboard use (⌘K, ⌘J, [, Esc).

Why the look is built to last

Every color, size and spacing value is a named token defined once, and the screens read from those tokens. When the platform grows to the rest of the team and to the pages that are drawn but not redesigned yet, they inherit the same look without a new design pass. A change to the navy, for example, is one edit.

What stays

The vocabulary stays. Only the structure and the look change.

The redesign changes structure, not language. These things were deliberately kept:

  • Thomas's labels and the order of the sidebar groups
  • The classes A, B, C, D and LH
  • The seven Dashboard tabs
  • The Attack Plan, Brain and Outcome names
  • The prediction model and its confidence tiers
  • The four trust states from the existing evidence ledger

Some areas are drawn in the sidebar but not redesigned yet. Map, Outreach, Phone, Email, Texting, LinkedIn, Social, Marketing, Website, More and System appear as disabled items with the tooltip "Not in this proposal yet". Mobile, roles and backend work are outside this proposal.
